body.statement:
Let \(\widehat h(t)=\int_{\mathcal A}e^{ita}h(a)\,da\).  For every fixed \(\rho>0\) there are constants \(c,C,C_0>0\), depending only on \(B_A,\beta,\rho\), such that every \(h\in H^\beta(\mathbb R)\) supported in \(\mathcal A\), with \(\|h\|_{H^\beta}\le R\), \(\|h\|_1\le M\), and \(\|\widehat h\|_{L^2[-\rho,\rho]}\le\varepsilon\), satisfies, for every integer \(k\ge1\),
\[
 \|h\|_\infty\le C\left[Rk^{1/2-\beta}+k(C_0k)^k\varepsilon+Mk e^{-ck}\right].
\]
Consequently, for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\),
\[
 \|h\|_\infty\le C(R+M)\left\{\frac{\log\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\right\}^{\beta-1/2}.
\]
body.proof_tex:
Put \(H(z)=\int_{-B_A}^{B_A}e^{iza}h(a)\,da\).  Absolute convergence and differentiation under the integral give
\[
 H^{(j)}(z)=\int_{-B_A}^{B_A}(ia)^j e^{iza}h(a)\,da,
 \qquad |H^{(j)}(0)|\le M B_A^j .
\]
Let \(T_k(z)=\sum_{j=0}^kH^{(j)}(0)z^j/j!\).  Taylor's formula, applied inside the integral, yields the two bounds
\[
 |H(t)-T_k(t)|\le M\frac{(B_A|t|)^{k+1}}{(k+1)!},
 \qquad t\in\mathbb R. \tag{1}
\]
We next record the elementary polynomial extrapolation inequality
\[
 sup_{|t|\le T}|p(t)|
 \le C\rho^{-1/2}\left(\frac{C(1+T)}{\rho}\right)^k
 \|p\|_{L^2[-\rho,\rho]},\qquad T\ge\rho, \tag{2}
\]
for every polynomial \(p\) of degree at most \(k\).  To verify (2), rescale to \([-1,1]\), expand \(p\) in the orthonormal Legendre basis, use Cauchy--Schwarz for its coefficients, and use the explicit three-term recursion to obtain \(|P_j(x)|\le(2|x|+1)^j\) for \(|x|\ge1\).  Summing the resulting geometric bound for \(0\le j\le k\) proves (2), including its displayed constants.

Apply (2) to \(T_k\).  On \([-\rho,\rho]\), (1) and the hypothesis give
\[
 \|T_k\|_2\le\varepsilon+(2\rho)^{1/2}M\frac{(B_A\rho)^{k+1}}{(k+1)!}. \tag{3}
\]
Choose a fixed \(a_0>0\), depending only on \(B_A\) and \(\rho\), small enough that \(T=a_0k\) makes both
\[
 \left\{C(1+T)/\rho\right\}^k\frac{(B_A\rho)^{k+1}}{(k+1)!}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \frac{(B_AT)^{k+1}}{(k+1)!}
\]
at most \(Ce^{-ck}\).  This follows directly from \((k+1)!\ge((k+1)/e)^{k+1}\), which itself follows by integrating \(\log x\) from \(1\) to \(k+1\).  Equations (1)--(3) therefore imply
\[
 sup_{|t|\le T}|H(t)|\le (C_0k)^k\varepsilon+CMe^{-ck}. \tag{4}
\]
Because \(\beta>1/2\), Fourier inversion is absolutely convergent.  Cauchy--Schwarz and the definition of the Sobolev norm give
\[
 \int_{|t|>T}|H(t)|\,dt
 \le \left\{\int_{|t|>T}(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2}\|h\|_{H^\beta}
 \le CR T^{1/2-\beta}. \tag{5}
\]
Splitting the inversion integral at \(T=a_0k\), and applying (4) and (5), proves the first assertion.

Finally let \(L=\log(1/\varepsilon)\) and choose
\[
 k=\left\lfloor c_1\frac{L}{\log(e+L)}\right\rfloor
\]
with \(c_1>0\) sufficiently small.  Then \(k(C_0k)^k\varepsilon\le Ck^{1/2-\beta}\) and \(ke^{-ck}\le Ck^{1/2-\beta}\) for all sufficiently large \(L\).  Since \(k\asymp L/\log L\), substitution into the first assertion proves the claimed logarithmic modulus.
